---
title: "Advanced: `filter=True`"
---

```{python}
#| label: setup-filtering-error-rows
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Setup: the demo's `Orders` schema, which every example on this page uses"
#| output: false
import dagster as dg
import polars as pl
from dagster_polars import PolarsParquetIOManager

import dagster_dataframely as dd
from dagster_dataframely_demo._data import storefront_orders
from dagster_dataframely_demo.schema import Orders


@dg.asset
def raw_orders() -> pl.DataFrame:
    return storefront_orders()
```

With `filter=True`, a run writes the rows that failed an `"error"` rule to a separate table, the error rows.
It writes every other row to the asset's table, and the run succeeds.
[Validation](validation.qmd) covers the default, and this page covers what `filter=True` changes:

- **The package writes the rows that failed an `"error"` rule under `<name>__error_rows`**, and writes the rest of the frame to the table.
  `error_rows_key` sets another key.
- **The run succeeds** when some rows fail an `"error"` rule, and fails with `NoValidRowsError` when every row does.
- **No rule's check is blocking**, but a failing `"error"` rule's check still fails at `ERROR`, so the asset shows "Degraded".
- **The materialization** reports the error-rows address, count and sample.
- **The asset gets a `context` parameter**, and a direct invocation needs `DAGSTER_DATAFRAMELY_ERROR_ROWS_DIR`.

<!-- rumdl-disable-next-line MD078 -->
```{mermaid}
%%| label: filtering-error-rows-outcomes
flowchart TD
    F["the decorated function returns"] --> N{"None?"}
    N -- yes --> SKIP["skip: nothing written<br/>every check passes<br/>run succeeds"]
    N -- no --> CS{"column schema matches?"}
    CS -- no --> DRIFT["nothing written<br/>dy_schema__columns fails<br/>run fails, ColumnSchemaError"]
    CS -- yes --> FILTER["Schema.filter"]
    FILTER --> ERR{"a row failed an 'error' rule?"}
    ERR -- no --> CLEAN["every row written<br/>error rows written empty<br/>run succeeds"]
    ERR -- yes --> WRITTEN["error rows written"]
    WRITTEN --> LEFT{"any other rows?"}
    LEFT -- no --> NONE["table not written<br/>run fails, NoValidRowsError"]
    LEFT -- yes --> PARTIAL["the other rows written<br/>'error' checks fail at ERROR, not blocking<br/>run succeeds"]
```

The package writes the error rows before anything can raise, so they are written however the run ends.
Then it writes every row that passed every `"error"` rule to the table, including the rows that failed only `"warn"` rules.
The two tables never share a row, so their row counts add up to the frame's.

| what the function returned | the table | the error rows | failing checks | run |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| columns or dtypes that are not the schema's | not written | not written | the column-schema check | fails, `ColumnSchemaError` |
| no row failed an `"error"` rule | every row | written empty | each `"warn"` rule's check, at `WARN` | succeeds |
| some rows failed an `"error"` rule | every other row | the rows that failed an `"error"` rule | `"error"` rules at `ERROR`, `"warn"` rules at `WARN`, none blocking | succeeds |
| every row failed an `"error"` rule | not written | every row | the same | fails, `NoValidRowsError` |
| `None`, meaning no source data | skipped | not written | none | succeeds |

**A run where every row fails an `"error"` rule still fails.**
It writes no table rather than an empty one, so an empty table never replaces the last-known-good table.
It writes every row under `<name>__error_rows` before it raises `NoValidRowsError`, so you can read them after the run fails.

![The Checks tab for an asset with `filter=True` after some rows failed. The selected check is non-blocking, and it shows its rendered constraint, the rule's expression, and the rows that failed the rule.](../assets/images/error-rows-checks.png)

## The asset's IO manager writes the error rows

`filter=True` is the whole setup.
There is no directory to configure and no second asset to declare.

The asset's own IO manager writes the error rows, under the asset's key with `__error_rows` added to the end.
It writes the error rows of `analytics/orders` to `analytics/orders__error_rows`.
This works with any IO manager that stores by asset key ([ADR-0006](https://github.com/ozanozbeker/dagster-dataframely/blob/main/docs/pre-1.0.md#adr-0006-the-assets-own-io-manager-writes-the-quarantine)).

The same declaration writes the error rows to a different place under each IO manager:

```{python}
#| label: filtering-error-rows-1
@dd.asset(Orders, filter=True)
def orders(raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return raw_orders
```

| IO manager | where it writes the error rows |
| --- | --- |
| `PolarsParquetIOManager` | `orders__error_rows.parquet`, in the same directory as `orders.parquet` |
| `DuckDBPolarsIOManager` | the table `orders__error_rows`, in the same schema as `orders` |

The first is a `UPathIOManager` and the second is a `DbIOManager`.
Nearly every first-party IO manager subclasses one of the two.

The error rows have the original columns, then one `String` rule column per rule, with `valid`, `invalid` or `unknown` in each row.
A rule column has the check name its rule gets at the default `rule` granularity, such as `dy_rule__amount__min`.
At `column` or `schema` granularity, use the rule column, not a check, to find the rows that failed a rule.
Check samples have at most `max_failure_samples` rows per rule, so the rule columns are the only complete record of which rules each row failed.

The error rows are not in the format `FailureInfo.write_parquet` writes, so `FailureInfo.read_parquet` and `FailureInfo.scan_parquet` cannot read them.
Both read the names of the rule columns from the parquet metadata key `rule_columns`.
The package passes the error rows to the asset's IO manager, which can write them to a database table.
A database table has no parquet metadata to hold that key.
The rule columns also have check names, not the name Dataframely gives each rule, such as `amount|min`.

The table's materialization has the error-rows address, the number of error rows, and which sets of rules they failed together.
See [What a run produces](what-a-run-produces.qmd).

**A run with no error rows writes them empty**, so they no longer hold the last run's rows.
Empty error rows have the same columns as error rows with rows.
So error rows that exist do not mean rows failed.
Read their row count, or check whether the materialization has `dataframely/error_rows_count`.

**A partitioned asset on a database IO manager needs `partition_expr`.**
`DbIOManager` raises an error without it, so you already set it for the asset's own table.
The error-rows write uses the same value.

**`filter=True` adds a `context` parameter to the asset**, whether or not the decorated function declares one.
The package needs the context to write the error rows.
So direct invocation of the asset needs a `dg.build_asset_context()` as the first argument.
See [Testing an asset](testing-an-asset.qmd).
An asset with `filter=False` keeps the signature you wrote.

## Two keywords change the key and the IO manager

`error_rows_key` sets the error-rows key.
`error_rows_io_manager_key` names the resource key of the IO manager that writes the error rows in a run.
Both need `filter=True`.
With `filter=False`, `dd.asset` raises `dg.DagsterInvalidDefinitionError` where you declare the asset.
Neither is a setting, so no `DAGSTER_DATAFRAMELY_*` variable sets them.

```{python}
#| label: filtering-error-rows-2
from dagster_duckdb_polars import DuckDBPolarsIOManager


@dd.asset(
    Orders,
    filter=True,
    error_rows_key=["audit", "orders__error_rows"],
    error_rows_io_manager_key="audit",
)
def audited_orders(raw_orders: pl.DataFrame) -> pl.DataFrame:
    return raw_orders


defs = dg.Definitions(
    assets=[raw_orders, audited_orders, dd.error_rows_spec(Orders, audited_orders)],
    resources={
        "io_manager": PolarsParquetIOManager(base_dir="data/warehouse"),
        "audit": DuckDBPolarsIOManager(database="data/warehouse.duckdb"),
    },
)
```

```{python}
#| label: filtering-error-rows-3
#| echo: false
#| output: false
# The cell above only declares the asset, so the build runs it here and checks what the page states.
import tempfile

import duckdb

from dagster_dataframely_demo._data import marketplace_orders


@dg.asset(name="raw_orders")
def marketplace_raw() -> pl.DataFrame:
    return marketplace_orders()


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    checked = dg.materialize(
        [marketplace_raw, audited_orders],
        resources={
            "io_manager": PolarsParquetIOManager(base_dir=tmp),
            "audit": DuckDBPolarsIOManager(database=f"{tmp}/warehouse.duckdb"),
        },
    )
    (event,) = [
        e
        for e in checked.get_asset_materialization_events()
        if e.asset_key == audited_orders.key
    ]
    metadata = event.step_materialization_data.materialization.metadata
    assert metadata["dataframely/error_rows_address"] == dg.MetadataValue.text(
        "audit/orders__error_rows"
    )
    with duckdb.connect(f"{tmp}/warehouse.duckdb") as connection:
        written = connection.sql("select count(*) from audit.orders__error_rows")
        assert written.fetchone() == (8,)
```

`PolarsParquetIOManager` writes the table to `audited_orders.parquet`.
`DuckDBPolarsIOManager` writes the error rows to the table `orders__error_rows` in the schema `audit`.
The error-rows address is `audit/orders__error_rows`.

**`dd.asset` adds `error_rows_io_manager_key` to the asset's `required_resource_keys`.**
So loading the definitions raises if no resource has that key.
The IO manager receives its own config and the asset's definition metadata, such as `partition_expr`.

**A database IO manager reads the schema from the metadata first.**
`DbIOManager` takes the schema from `metadata["schema"]`, then from its own `schema` config, then from the key prefix.
So `error_rows_key` changes the schema only when the asset has no `schema` metadata and the IO manager has no `schema` config.
The table name is always the key's last part.

**The collision check reads the error-rows key.**
Before the decorated function runs, a run raises `ErrorRowsKeyCollisionError` if another asset materializes the key `error_rows_key` sets.
The run also raises when that key is the asset's own key.

**A direct invocation writes under `error_rows_dir`, at a path built from the error-rows key.**
It has no IO manager, so `error_rows_io_manager_key` changes nothing there.
Dagster still checks the asset's required resources, so pass a value for that resource key, such as `dg.build_asset_context(resources={"audit": None})`.

## `error_rows_spec` adds the error rows to the asset graph

They are a record of a run.
They are not in the asset graph, so no asset can depend on them until you add them with `error_rows_spec`:

```{python}
#| label: filtering-error-rows-4
defs = dg.Definitions(
    assets=[raw_orders, orders, dd.error_rows_spec(Orders, orders)],
    resources={"io_manager": PolarsParquetIOManager(base_dir="data/warehouse")},
)
```

![The lineage view shows the error rows' node. Its one edge comes from `marketing_orders`, the asset with `filter=True`, not from the upstream `raw_marketplace_orders`. Dagster draws the node with a dashed border because it is an external asset, and it shows the materialization that the step of `marketing_orders` logged.](../assets/images/error-rows-lineage.png)

`error_rows_spec` returns a `dg.AssetSpec` keyed `orders__error_rows` that depends on `orders` and has its own Columns tab.
It has no compute function, because the decorator already writes the rows.
It has the `polars` kind, as the asset does, but none of the asset's other kinds.
To add a storage kind such as `duckdb`, call `.merge_attributes(kinds={"duckdb"})` on the spec.
The IO manager that wrote the rows also loads them for a downstream asset that names the error rows as an input.

**The error rows' Columns tab has no column constraints.**
It lists the schema's columns with their dtypes, descriptions and tags, then one `String` column per rule.
The error rows can fail any of the schema's constraints, so a `not null` on a column full of nulls would be false.
The primary key is absent too, because rows with a duplicate key are among the error rows.

Pass `error_rows_spec` the asset definition, and the spec uses its partitions, its asset group, its owners and its tags.
So the catalog lists the error rows in the same group as the asset.
The spec drops the asset's `dagster/kind/` tags, because Dagster stores each kind as one of those tags.
The spec also uses the error-rows key, the IO manager key and the definition metadata the writer used, so a downstream asset loads the rows from where they were written.
`dd.asset` records the first two in the definition metadata, under `dataframely/error_rows_key` and `dataframely/error_rows_io_manager_key`.
Pass an asset key instead, and set the partitions with `partitions_def=`.
The spec then has `<name>__error_rows` and Dagster's default IO manager key, `io_manager`, so call `.with_io_manager_key()` on it for an asset whose IO manager has another key.
Passing both an asset definition and `partitions_def=` raises `dg.DagsterInvariantViolationError`.

`group_name=` sets the error rows' group.
With an asset definition, it overrides the asset's group and does not raise.
For example, pass `group_name="error_rows"` on every call to list every asset's error rows in one group.
With an asset key and no `group_name=`, the error rows are in the `default` group.

`owners=` and `tags=` follow the same rule.
With an asset definition, each replaces the asset's value whole, so `owners=[]` removes the asset's owners and `tags={}` removes its tags.
With an asset key, the error rows have the owners and tags these set, and the `polars` kind.

**With the spec, every write materializes the error rows.**
The asset's own step logs the materialization after the IO manager writes the rows.
It logs one for each outcome that writes them: a clean run's empty write, a run where some rows failed, and the write before `NoValidRowsError`.
The materialization has the IO manager's metadata for the write, such as `path` or `dagster/table_name`, and the row count.
The row count is under `dagster/partition_row_count` for a partition, and under `dagster/row_count` otherwise.

```{python}
#| label: filtering-error-rows-5
import tempfile

from dagster_dataframely_demo._data import marketplace_orders


@dg.asset(name="raw_orders")
def marketplace_raw() -> pl.DataFrame:
    return marketplace_orders()


with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmp:
    result = dg.materialize(
        [marketplace_raw, orders, dd.error_rows_spec(Orders, orders)],
        resources={"io_manager": PolarsParquetIOManager(base_dir=tmp)},
    )

{
    event.asset_key.to_user_string(): event.materialization.metadata[
        "dagster/row_count"
    ].value
    for event in result.get_asset_materialization_events()
}
```

The error rows then have a materialization history, so a downstream asset can automate on them.
See [Automation](partitioning.qmd#automation).

**Without the spec, a run launched from a code location records no materialization for the error rows**, so the catalog does not list them as an asset with no definition.
A run of `dg.materialize` or `execute_in_process` has no code location to read, so it records the materialization with or without the spec.

## `error_rows_dir` is for calling, not running

Direct invocation has no step, so there is no IO manager to write the error rows.
Instead, `file_writer` writes them under the directory `DAGSTER_DATAFRAMELY_ERROR_ROWS_DIR` sets.
A run does not use this directory.

```bash
DAGSTER_DATAFRAMELY_ERROR_ROWS_DIR=/tmp/error_rows
```

The package reads the directory when it writes the error rows, not when the module imports.
So a `monkeypatch.setenv` in a test takes effect even though Python imported the module that defines the asset earlier.
A call with no error rows never reads it and writes no file.

If the variable is unset, a call with error rows raises `ErrorRowsDirError`.
There is no default directory.

There is no per-asset override, for the reason [the out-of-scope record](https://github.com/ozanozbeker/dagster-dataframely/blob/main/docs/out-of-scope/error-rows-dir-argument.md) gives.

Under that directory, the file path follows `UPathIOManager`'s layout, built from the error-rows key and the partition key:

```text
<error_rows_dir>/<key part>/.../<name>__error_rows.parquet
<error_rows_dir>/<key part>/.../<name>__error_rows/<partition>.parquet
```

Each partition is a separate file in a `<name>__error_rows/` directory, so a backfill of one partition rewrites one file.
The file is always parquet, so it keeps every dtype the schema declares.

The package formats a multi-partition key as its dimension keys joined by `/`, in dimension-name order.
It escapes a partition key containing `..` or a leading `/`, instead of rejecting it, so no partition can write a file outside `error_rows_dir`.
